title: Using Hinge Point Questions in English
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau, extracting from his book Bringing the English Curriculum to Life, explains how to design effective hinge-point multiple-choice questions (MCQs) for English lessons. A hinge question is a fast diagnostic check -- answerable in under two minutes, readable by the teacher in about thirty seconds -- deployed at the exact moment a teacher needs to know whether to move on or reteach. Didau walks through several worked examples from poetry (Wilfred Owen) and drama (An Inspector Calls), showing how well-designed distractors must be plausible and rooted in genuine misconceptions rather than absurd or obviously wrong, and how questions with more than one defensible correct answer can open up structured classroom discussion. He argues for using two or three distractors rather than piling on more, since the marginal statistical benefit of extra distractors is outweighed by the cost of writing them well. The piece closes with a summary of research evidence supporting hinge questions across settings from Black & Wiliam's foundational studies to university-level statistics courses, and a ready-made ChatGPT prompt for generating hinge questions on any topic.
points: Didau's design principle -- distractors must be plausible and rooted in real misconceptions, not absurd 'Mickey Mouse wrote Romeo and Juliet' options -- is the difference between a diagnostic question and a guessing game.

His worked example on Wilfred Owen's 'Exposure' shows how two equally 'true' but incomplete distractors can be used deliberately to spark structured discussion about which answer is most accurate, not just which is correct.

He gives a hard operational constraint -- students answer in under two minutes, teachers read all responses in about thirty seconds -- that turns the abstract idea of 'checking understanding' into something usable mid-lesson via mini-whiteboards.

His recommendation to cap distractors at two or three, rather than maximising them for statistical rigor, is a practical trade-off between question quality and the time cost of writing good wrong answers.

Citing evidence from Black & Wiliam (1998) through to Zimmaro (2010) situates a very English-specific technique within a decades-long, cross-subject research base for formative diagnostic questioning.
quotes: A hinge question is a diagnostic tool deployed at a point in a lesson – the hinge – where teachers need to know whether students are ready to move on require further instruction.
Students need to be able to answer the hinge question quickly – ideally in less than two minutes – and teachers should be able to read and interpret answers in about 30 seconds.
The aim should be to eliminate guessing: students who know the answer should get it right; students who don’t know the answer should be distracted by one of the distractors.
One of the keys of writing distractors is that they should be plausible and expose potential errors in students’ understanding.
And remember, if students are guessing, the hinge question probably is not well designed.
Black & Wiliam (1998) found that using hinge point questions in a classroom setting helped teachers identify students’ misunderstandings and adjust their teaching methods accordingly.
